title: Everything You Need to Know About AI Tokens
dek: An Operator's Cut with Nufar Gaspar on the term that's dominating every enterprise AI conversation: the token. From the all-inclusive era to token-maxing leaderboards to today's anxiety-driven self-censorship, this is the primer on what a token actually is, why the bill is so hard to read, and how to spend wisely rather than sparingly.

oneIdea.headline: Spend tokens wisely, not sparingly — and measure cost per accepted task, not cost per token.
oneIdea.summary: After the all-inclusive, token-maxing, and now token-anxious eras, the goal is the token-smart era. Understand what a token really is, recognize that tokens aren't born equal across labs and layers, and stop reading the bill in tokens — which are an unmeterable moving target — and start reading it in dollars per accepted task. Kill the tokens that spin, tune the tokens that produce, and fearlessly defend the tokens that teach.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: Your scribe is on a flat fee today. This edition explains why that may not hold.
items.body: Almost every ambient scribe sold into UK general practice is priced per clinician per month, which makes budgeting easy and hides the meter entirely. The edition's own numbers show why that pricing is fragile: agentic work runs five to thirty times the tokens of a simple chat, and when Anthropic reissued Opus in April the price sheet was unchanged while the same text produced about thirty per cent more tokens. If Whittemore is right, inference keeps getting cheaper and the flat fee survives. If Zitron is right, the subsidy is withdrawn and per-seat becomes per-use. Neither requires action now, but it is worth knowing your notice period and whether renewal locks the current price, before the conversation is had for you.

items.title: The self-censoring clinician is the real cost, not the tokens
items.body: The best line in the edition is Nufar Gaspar's: the most expensive token is the one your best person is afraid to spend. Translated to a surgery, that is the partner who stops using the scribe on the complicated twenty-minute consultation — precisely where it saves the most time and where the note matters most — because a complex case feels extravagant. The arithmetic says the opposite. An email-length exchange costs roughly half a penny; the deep, messy consultation is exactly what you bought the thing for. If a colleague is rationing, the fix is telling them the actual unit cost, not adding a policy.

items.title: Cost per accepted task has a clean clinical translation
items.body: The edition's central metric — cost per accepted task, counting retries and correction rather than raw consumption — maps almost exactly onto the only scribe question worth asking: what proportion of notes go into the record without meaningful editing? That is measurable in an afternoon. Take twenty consultations across two clinicians, record whether each draft was accepted unchanged, lightly edited, or rewritten, and note the minutes spent correcting. It gives a number for the next contract discussion and, more usefully, tells you whether the tool is stronger in some consultation types than others. The same logic applies to Medical Examiner work, where the acceptable error rate on a scrutiny summary is effectively zero and a draft that needs checking line by line has saved nothing.

the_other_side.source: The More You Buy, The More You Lose
the_other_side.text: This edition's premise is that token spend is a management problem — spend wisely, measure cost per accepted task, and the arithmetic comes good. Zitron, five days earlier, argued that the arithmetic does not come good at any level of discipline, because the price you are quoted is not the cost of the thing. His evidence is that heavy usage destroys the seller, not the buyer: Anthropic and OpenAI, he writes, "allow users to burn $8000 to $14,000 a month for $200", and GitHub Copilot only reached scale by letting subscribers "burn more than 25 times their monthly subscription fee" — with user revolts when metered billing arrived. He notes that NVIDIA's promised twenty-five-fold cut in inference cost has been quietly pared back to ten, and that even that has made no AI company profitable. His conclusion is that "using AI only seems to be getting more expensive" for everyone in the chain, and that a cost-per-accepted-task discipline optimises a number that is subsidised in the first place.

the_truth_beneath.text: Both men orbit one variable: whether the price of a unit of AI work reflects what it costs to produce. They agree on more than the framing suggests — tokens are opaque, agentic work multiplies consumption several-fold, and the heaviest users pay a small fraction of what they consume. The empirical question that will resolve is whether inference gets cheap enough to be simultaneously profitable to sell and worth buying; the observable that settles it is published inference gross margins and whether the flat-rate heavy-use plans survive without conversion to metered billing. The residue is pure worldview: whether discipline is the answer or the distraction. Whittemore is vindicated if measured cost per accepted task falls while capability holds and vendors still make money. Zitron is vindicated if the subsidy is withdrawn and the true price makes the work uneconomic. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is that both now say the sticker price tells you nothing. Watch whether flat-rate plans quietly become metered.

headlines.headline: Every room is having the same token conversation
headlines.summary: Practitioners feel watched when they use an expensive model, regular users wonder if one ambitious prompt will eat their weekly allowance, and leadership sees a bill growing faster than expected. Nufar's aim is to flip that anxiety into literacy — understand what the bill means, then spend wisely rather than sparingly.

headlines.headline: OpenAI's CFO wants a 'Useful Intelligence Per Dollar' scorecard
headlines.summary: The proposed metric is built around one question: what does each successful task actually cost? That reframes tokens away from a purely financial number and toward where usage creates value versus where it quietly leaks it.

headlines.headline: The four eras of token consumption
headlines.summary: We started token-oblivious in the all-inclusive era, where flat subscriptions hid the meter. Then came token-maxing (usage as a badge of AI maturity), then today's token-anxious backlash — and the goal now is the token-smart era.

headlines.headline: The leaderboard era: 'Claudenomics' and $500M bills
headlines.summary: Meta tracked employee AI usage on an internal leaderboard, burning 60-74 trillion tokens in a single month with its top user hitting 280 billion (~2.3M books). Uber blew through its entire 2026 AI coding budget in four months, and one unnamed company ran up a $500M Claude bill with no limits in place.

headlines.headline: Overspending beats underspending on a one-year timescale
headlines.summary: NLW: the hand-wringing over gamed leaderboards is overwrought — of course people game systems with real stakes. He'll bet any amount that a company wildly overspending via a token leaderboard will be farther ahead than one that underspends out of fear of proving ROI.

headlines.headline: Even the token-maxers are now token-minimizing
headlines.summary: Meta went from a leaderboard to a memo constraining AI usage — the press now calls it token-minimizing — and Uber caps employees at 1,500. When employees self-censor, every prompt becomes an ROI conversation, which is exactly the wrong era to stay in.

headlines.headline: The most expensive token is the one your best person is afraid to spend.
headlines.summary: Nufar's framing for why token anxiety is dangerous: self-censorship pushes your most capable people back toward low-stakes work instead of the high-value workflows that actually move the needle.

headlines.headline: What a token actually is
headlines.summary: A token is a chunk of text — bigger than a character, usually smaller than a word — that the model reads and writes. In English the ratio is roughly three-quarters of a word per token, so a page of text is about 1,000 tokens. OpenAI's public tokenizer page lets you see how your own text gets chunked.

headlines.headline: The 'language tax' on non-English prompts
headlines.summary: Because billing is per token, languages like Hindi, Thai, and Greek can generate two to five times more tokens for the same content — so the same question costs much more in another language. Code has its own quirks, with indentation, brackets, and whitespace all becoming tokens.

headlines.headline: The strawberry test is a tokenizer feature, not a failure
headlines.summary: Models fail to count the R's in 'strawberry' because they never saw the individual letters — just 'straw' and 'berry' as tokens. Many of the 'AI is so dumb' memes are literally just tokenization artifacts.

headlines.headline: What everyday work actually costs in tokens
headlines.summary: An email is ~500-700 tokens (about half a cent — nobody should ration those), a page is ~1,000, images run just over 1,000, and deep research can hit tens or hundreds of thousands. One learner accidentally sent a yes/no question to a deep-research tool that spawned ~100 sub-agents and cost over 4 million tokens.

headlines.headline: Every conversation turn compounds
headlines.summary: The model doesn't remember prior messages, so it re-sends the entire session each turn. By turn ten it may be reprocessing so much earlier context that total tokens grow far faster than the number of turns suggests — immortal sessions quietly balloon the bill.

headlines.headline: Higher-value use cases inherently consume more tokens
headlines.summary: NLW: the direction of travel is clear — more advanced, more useful work requires more intelligence and thus more tokens. Unaddressed token anxiety incentivizes people to stay swimming in daily emails instead of doing the deep research and agentic work leaders actually want.

headlines.headline: Agentic work runs 5-30x the tokens of a simple chat
headlines.summary: Agents work autonomously in loops, and a typical task involves 10-20 model calls carrying instructions, history, tool definitions, and prior results. McKinsey estimates ~60% of an agentic task's cost is tied to checking, refining, and regenerating answers — the expensive part is getting from the answer to the accepted result.

headlines.headline: Tokens aren't born equal across labs
headlines.summary: Every lab has its own tokenizer — OpenAI's vocabulary is ~200k, Gemini's ~256k, Llama's about half, Claude's unpublished. Since price per million is denominated in each lab's own tokens, the same document can cost 10-20% more on one provider than another, making the sticker price meaningless for comparison.

headlines.headline: Opus 4.7's 'shrinkflation': same price, 30% more tokens
headlines.summary: When Opus 4.7 shipped in April, the per-million price sheet was identical but a new tokenizer produced ~30% more tokens for the same text. Independent analysis of over a million requests found native token counts up 32-45%, with real-world bills up 12-27% after caching. Same sticker, smaller candy bar.

headlines.headline: Every request has three token layers, priced very differently
headlines.summary: Input tokens (prompt, history, files, tool definitions) are cheapest but accumulate fast; reasoning tokens are the model's invisible internal thinking, billed at the high output rate and adding 4-20x; output tokens are what you see, typically 3-5x pricier than input. The reasoning layer — like 'kitchen time' on a restaurant bill — catches everyone by surprise.

headlines.headline: More reasoning effort doesn't always mean better answers
headlines.summary: High reasoning effort can drive 10-12x more tokens, but for simple questions lower reasoning often produces a lower cost per task and better quality by preventing the model from overthinking. The GPT-5-class gap is widening too — $10 per million input vs. $50 output.

headlines.headline: The cheaper model can be more expensive to operate
headlines.summary: Databricks tested coding agents on its own code base: Sonnet 5 was 1.7x cheaper per token than Opus 4.8, but cost ~$2.09 per task versus $1.94 for Opus because it needed more iterations. The lesson: reach for the right model, not the cheapest. Different agent harnesses at the same quality also showed a 2x+ difference in cost per task.

headlines.headline: Cost per accepted task is the only metric that compares
headlines.summary: Include retries, review, and every correction, then divide by accepted results — that's your cost per accepted task. The practical audit: run 5-10 representative tasks through your model and tool options, hold input and quality constant, and compare first-pass success, human correction, elapsed time, and total cost.

headlines.headline: Three kinds of tokens: teach, produce, spin
headlines.summary: Tokens that teach (experiments, failed workflows, identity files, memory) are tuition and should be defended fearlessly. Tokens that produce ship real work. Tokens that spin — machines talking to themselves, idle agents, bloated context, wrong-model use — are activity without output. The token-smart move: kill the spin, tune production, protect teaching, in that order.

headlines.headline: Nufar's $1,500 machine talking to itself
headlines.summary: Her disabled 'Chloe' chief-of-staff agent ran on the Anthropic API with bills going to a secondary inbox. Traveling and not using it, she still got charged — $1,500 in two weeks, ~400 million tokens in and near-zero out (a ~2,600:1 ratio) from cron jobs compacting empty sessions every 30 minutes. If it happened to an AI expert, it can happen to anyone whose company owns the card.

headlines.headline: Spin isn't only mistakes — it's things that quietly stopped being worth it
headlines.summary: NLW ran an OpenClaw agent perpetually researching new AI adoption data sources; it did exactly what it was told but simply wasn't valuable enough for the cost. Auditing spin means catching processes that accidentally became spin — like hourly Slack miners or a morning brief nobody reads — not just outright errors.

headlines.headline: The usual suspects for silent token spend
headlines.summary: Watch idle or over-frequent agents, unused automations, the 'pre-prompt tax' of always-on rules and tool definitions, immortal conversations, unfiltered data retrieval (500 rows when you needed 20), scattered context, and rework loops. Diagnostics include the weekend test, extreme input-to-output ratios, and spend rising while value stays flat.

headlines.headline: Six habits anyone can adopt to mind their tokens
headlines.summary: New task means new session; be intentional about model choice; rightsize context (Goldilocks, not too much or little); build reusable skills and automations instead of ad hoc re-asking; filter everything you can; and kill jobs early when the model's reasoning shows it's off, rather than letting it spin.

headlines.headline: Use /doctor to audit your own setup
headlines.summary: Anthropic's Claude Code /doctor command audits token distribution, stale skills, redundant tool configs, and overly long or overlapping instructions, returning concrete kill/reduce recommendations. Non-Claude users can have their AI recreate the same audit — it isn't complex.

headlines.headline: Model routing is still very early — and preferences still matter
headlines.summary: NLW expects routing norms to be solved first for deterministic software engineering and to stay far messier for knowledge work, where preference is about the nature of a response, not benchmark scores. The GPT-5 auto-router frustrated super users — proof people want control — so understanding model capabilities remains a high-leverage skill.

headlines.headline: Defend the learning budget, don't just cut the bill
headlines.summary: The point isn't only driving the bill down but improving return — and that often means spending more on tokens that teach: running the same task three ways, experimenting with tools and skills, and building context so the model gives personalized, organization-aware results. A 20k-developer study found the heaviest AI users were roughly twice as productive.

headlines.headline: For orgs: make usage visible, then tier the budget
headlines.summary: Make consumption visible and teach people to spend smartly, not sparingly. Budget by workload and individual — someone building reusable skills for the whole team deserves far more than someone using AI as an extended Google — and audit on a schedule for stale automations and instructions.
